answer_text:
Here is a comprehensive guide on how to **avoid fake job scams**, especially important as reported job-related scams jumped more than 1,000 percent between May and late July 2025:

---

## 🔍 1. Research the Company Thoroughly
Scammers often create fake job listings that appear legitimate. Always check the official employer website to see if the job is listed there. If it's not, it might be a scam. You can also look up the employer on Google and LinkedIn to make sure it's real and has actual employees.

---

## 📧 2. Scrutinize the Email Address and Communication
Be very suspicious of offers from Gmail, Yahoo, or similar personal email domains — legitimate recruiters typically use corporate email accounts. Scammers frequently fake emails with free web-based email accounts and use slightly modified versions of the official employer's domain name.

---

## 💰 3. Never Pay for a Job
Don't pay for the promise of a job. Honest employers, including the federal government, will never ask you to pay to get a job. Anyone who does is a scammer. Legitimate employers will never ask you to pay for job applications, training, or equipment. If someone wants you to send money, it's a scam.

---

## 🚩 4. Watch Out for "Too Good to Be True" Offers
If a job offer seems too good to be true (enormous salary or fantastic perks with minimal effort required), it probably is. Be cautious of unrealistic promises — this is a common tactic used by scammers to lure people in. Nearly 80 percent of these scams target low-skill roles, using inflated pay and vague requirements as bait.

---

## ⚠️ 5. Don't Be Pressured by Urgency
Take your time. Fraudulent job employers will pressure you to act quickly by paying or sharing personal information with them. A real employer would not pressure you to make a quick decision. Recruiters insisting on urgency ("Please respond within 24 hours") could indicate a scam contact.

---

## 🔐 6. Protect Your Personal Information
Never provide sensitive personal information (your Social Security number or bank details) early in the hiring process. Legitimate employers usually wait to ask for this information until later — typically on the first day of work. Never provide your Tax ID number, bank details, or copies of your ID during initial conversations.

---

## 🏦 7. Beware of Fake Check Scams
Never bank on a "cleared" check. No honest potential employer will ever send you a check to deposit and then tell you to send on part of the money or buy gift cards with it — that's a fake check scam.

---

## 🔗 8. Be Careful with Links and Attachments
Avoid opening attachments from unknown senders via email, text message, or social media — it might be a scammer. Install antivirus software and update it regularly. Before sending any information to employers, make sure the website is secure, having a URL beginning with "HTTPS://" and not "HTTP://".

---

## ✅ 9. Verify Through Official Channels
Treat every unsolicited offer as unverified until proven otherwise. Ask for an email from the recruiter's corporate domain and a calendar invite from the same domain. If you're unsure, call the company's main line and ask to confirm the contact.

---

## 🕵️ 10. Watch for Vague Job Descriptions
Fake job postings often have vague requirements. Be cautious of opportunities that only ask for simple criteria, like being of legal age, being able to read, or knowing how to type. These broad qualifications may indicate the job is not genuine. Strive to look for more defined skills and experience requirements in job descriptions.

---

## 📣 11. Report Suspicious Offers
Save evidence. Screenshots, URLs, and message histories help platforms and companies take action. If something feels off, pause and validate — even a five-minute check can prevent a costly mistake. You can report job scams to the **Federal Trade Commission (FTC)** at [reportfraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov).

---

Stay vigilant and trust your instincts — if something feels off, it probably is. Take a step back and consult someone you trust. The greater the sense of urgency and the greater the opportunity, the more likely it is a scam.
